glossary.observation: Ice-wedge polygons in Alaska's Noatak tundra. Repeated thermal contraction cracking and ice growth organise the permafrost landscape.

glossary.def: Nearest point to the Sun. Early January. A few percent extra insolation, not the cause of seasons.
glossary.observation: Hubble observed Comet ISON on 2 November 2013, before its closest approach to the Sun. Perihelion names that closest orbital point; the coloured filters show coma and tail structure, not a map of the orbit.

glossary.def: Ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years. It may contain ice but need not be permanently ice-filled.
glossary.observation: Ice-wedge polygons in Alaska's Noatak tundra. Repeated thermal contraction cracking and ice growth organise the permafrost landscape.

glossary.def: Pressure-gradient force: the force per unit mass associated with a pressure difference, directed from higher towards lower pressure.
glossary.observation: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

glossary.def: The fraction of the near side that is sunlit, as seen from Earth.
glossary.observation: The Artemis II crew photographed this lunar crescent on 7 April 2026. Phase is the visible fraction of the sunlit hemisphere, not Earth's shadow.

glossary.def: The visible layer of the Sun from which most of its observed light escapes. Sunspots are relatively cooler, magnetically active regions within it.
glossary.observation: NASA SDO observation of active region AR 12192 in 2014. Sunspots are cooler areas of the photosphere; the orange display colour is image processing.

glossary.def: The use of light energy to build organic molecules from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen-producing photosynthesis transfers carbon into living matter.
glossary.observation: Forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon. Leaves intercept rain and absorb light for photosynthesis; the photograph shows the living store, not the invisible molecular reactions.

glossary.def: The aggressor that captures by headward erosion.
glossary.observation: Wutach Gorge, Germany. Capture diverted drainage from the Danube system towards the Rhine; subsequent incision cut this gorge.

glossary.def: Low, gently sloping, open land.
glossary.observation: Ahuriri River plain near Omarama, New Zealand. River deposition builds a relatively flat valley floor between higher ground.

glossary.def: A collection of particles orbiting a planet, ranging from fine dust to larger fragments. Saturn's rings consist mainly of water ice.
glossary.observation: Cassini, 6 October 2004: a natural-colour mosaic of Saturn and its rings. The rings are a thin disc of orbiting particles.

glossary.def: Elevated land with a relatively flat top.
glossary.observation: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

glossary.def: Deep hollow at the foot of a fall, scoured by falling water and load.
glossary.observation: Cwmorthin waterfall and plunge pool, Wales. Falling water and entrained sediment erode the pool below the step in the river bed.

glossary.def: Describing a river regime mainly controlled by rainfall; its discharge seasonality reflects rainfall and catchment storage.
glossary.observation: Floodwater on the Stillaguamish River, Washington. Rain-fed regimes respond to precipitation; a flow's competence is the largest sediment it can move, which cannot be inferred from water colour alone.

glossary.def: High-latitude cell. Rise near 60°, sink at the pole.
glossary.observation: GOES-East cloud observations over the Americas, 22 April 2014. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude systems provide evidence of atmospheric circulation. The three-cell pattern is a long-term zonal average, not three fixed cloud rings in this single image.

glossary.def: The pressure of water or gas within pores in soil or rock. Increasing water pressure can reduce effective stress and resistance to slope failure.
glossary.observation: Slumping above Redcliff Point, Dorset. Rotational movement displaces blocks along a curved shear surface; the surface scars and tilted ground provide evidence.

glossary.def: Bed hollow where pebbles swirl and abrade.
glossary.observation: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Sediment circulating in eddies abrades the bedrock, enlarging these potholes.

glossary.def: A number written as 10 raised to an exponent, used to express large or small quantities and compare their scales.
glossary.observation: NASA/ESA Hubble mosaic of Andromeda. Resolved stars and dust lanes provide an observed view of a galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away.

glossary.def: The informal span of Earth history before the Cambrian Period, covering the Hadean, Archaean and Proterozoic eons.
glossary.observation: Layered rocks at Grand Canyon record the geological carbon cycle and deep time. Lithification converts sediment into rock; the canyon also exposes much older basement in its inner gorge. A landscape photograph alone does not date individual beds.

glossary.def: A difference in pressure between two places. It creates a pressure-gradient force that can start air moving.
glossary.observation: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

glossary.def: How pressure changes with distance. Steep gradient, strong PGF, strong wind.
glossary.observation: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

glossary.def: The chosen zero of longitude. The modern reference meridian used by WGS84 lies about 102 m east of the historic Greenwich transit circle.
glossary.observation: The historic Greenwich Meridian makes a reference longitude tangible. Modern WGS84 zero longitude lies about 102 metres east of this line.

glossary.def: A rule for flattening the globe onto a plane. Every rule distorts something.
glossary.observation: NASA Blue Marble monthly composite in an equirectangular latitude–longitude grid. Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the equator; parallels run east–west. The geographic reference lines are mathematical, not marks on the land.

glossary.def: Fragmented material from explosive eruption: ash, pumice, blocks.
glossary.observation: USGS photograph of Pinatubo's Marella River valley, 1 July 1991. These are deposits left by pyroclastic flows, not a view of a flow in motion.

glossary.def: Sun and Moon at right angles as seen from Earth. Neap tide.
glossary.observation: A telescopic photograph of the first-quarter Moon on 9 July 2019. Near quadrature, the Sun and Moon lie about 90° apart in our sky.

glossary.def: Bedrock. Not soil.
glossary.observation: Rankosol over granite on Île de Berder, France. A shallow organic-rich surface over non-calcareous bedrock illustrates a ranker; horizons are real field layers, not a template.

glossary.def: Balloon-borne package that profiles temperature, humidity and pressure with height.
glossary.observation: Balloon-borne radiosondes transmit measurements of the atmosphere. Profiles of temperature, humidity and pressure help locate inversions and estimate lapse rates.

glossary.def: Dry region leeward of a barrier, after the air has already dropped water.
glossary.observation: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favour wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

glossary.def: Drop impact that detaches particles at the soil surface.
glossary.observation: USDA NRCS archive photograph of raindrop impact. Splash detaches and redistributes soil particles before surface runoff carries them farther.

glossary.def: Spiral band of showers and storms outside the eyewall.
glossary.observation: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

glossary.def: A former beach now above present sea level because of land uplift, a fall in sea level, or both.
glossary.observation: A raised beach near Northbank. Former shorelines record changes in relative sea level, which can include land uplift after unloading of ice.

glossary.def: A traditional soil term for a shallow, often acidic soil over hard, non-calcareous rock; commonly found on steep or exposed ground.
glossary.observation: Rankosol over granite on Île de Berder, France. A shallow organic-rich surface over non-calcareous bedrock illustrates a ranker; horizons are real field layers, not a template.

glossary.def: Water added to the aquifer, usually from rain and infiltration.
glossary.observation: Stream Passage Pot, Ingleborough, North Yorkshire. This entrance belongs to the Gaping Gill karst drainage system, where surface water enters underground passages.

glossary.def: The characteristic seasonal pattern of river discharge, influenced by rainfall, snowmelt, storage and human regulation.
glossary.observation: USGS gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica, 12 December 2001. Repeated measurements of stage and discharge produce a river's hydrograph.

glossary.def: The variation in elevation within an area, often expressed as the difference between its highest and lowest points.
glossary.observation: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

glossary.def: The typical time material remains in a store. For a well-mixed store at steady state, mean residence time is its amount divided by its outflow rate.
glossary.observation: Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, Arizona. Reservoir storage and controlled releases alter the timing and size of flows downstream.

glossary.def: Processes that release energy from organic matter. Aerobic respiration consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water.
glossary.observation: White beech leaf litter at Carowiry Creek, New South Wales. Organic material on the forest floor stores carbon and provides material for decomposition.

glossary.def: Where underground drainage returns to the surface.
glossary.observation: Groundwater emerges at a karst spring in Alabama. Water stored in connected pores and fractures can return to the surface as spring flow.

glossary.def: Shortening. Hanging wall up. Thrust if the plane is gentle.
glossary.observation: Reverse fault in layered igneous rock from Montana's Stillwater Complex. Trace matching layers across the break: the hanging wall moved up relative to the footwall.

glossary.def: One trip around the Sun. About 365.25 days. Not the same as rotation (the daily spin).
glossary.observation: SDO recorded Venus crossing the Sun's disc in June 2012. A transit is an observable alignment of orbiting bodies. Revolution means motion around another body; this time sequence is not a scale drawing of the orbits.

glossary.def: A path of constant compass bearing, shown as a straight line on a Mercator map. Except for special cases, it is not the shortest path on a sphere.
glossary.observation: NASA Blue Marble imagery reprojected by Mdf into Mercator. Local angles are preserved, area grows towards the poles, and a constant-bearing route plots as a straight line.

glossary.def: An elongated region where the lithosphere is extending and thinning. Some continental rifts develop into ocean basins; others cease spreading.
glossary.observation: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

glossary.def: Small erosional channel cut by running water. Can grow into a gully.
glossary.observation: Hillslope gully and sheet erosion near Charters Towers, Queensland, documented by CSIRO. Loss of cover exposes soil to runoff.

glossary.def: The increase in discharge as the catchment starts to contribute.
glossary.observation: USGS stream-gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica. A time series from a gauge reveals a hydrograph's rising limb, peak and falling limb. Lag time compares rainfall timing with the discharge peak; it is not a distance along the river.

glossary.def: Thick crust under a mountain, the submerged part of the raft.
glossary.observation: Roots grow through existing rock joints. Their growth can widen cracks, contributing to biological and physical weathering.

glossary.def: Earth spinning on its axis. One solar day ≈ 24 hours.
glossary.observation: South Africa at night, photographed from the ISS. Earth's rotation relative to the Sun defines the solar day; rotation relative to distant stars defines the slightly shorter sidereal day.

glossary.def: A slice of slope that rotates on a curved shear. Crown drops; toe shoves.
glossary.observation: Slumping above Redcliff Point, Dorset. Rotational movement displaces blocks along a curved shear surface; the surface scars and tilted ground provide evidence.

glossary.def: The maximum elevation reached by a wave above a specified reference sea level as it moves onto land; distinct from inland inundation distance.
glossary.observation: Coastal damage after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. Run-up is the maximum vertical elevation reached by the water above a reference sea level; survey evidence is needed to attach a number to this photograph.

glossary.def: A shear seismic wave with particle motion perpendicular to its travel direction. It propagates through solids but not through the liquid outer core.
glossary.observation: USGS seismometer installation in Puerto Rico. Wave arrival times and recorded ground motion are used to estimate an earthquake's focus, epicentre and magnitude; none of those buried locations is visible in this photograph.

glossary.def: A five-category hurricane scale based on maximum sustained wind speed. It does not rate rainfall, storm surge or the full impact of a cyclone.
glossary.observation: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

glossary.def: Salt content. More salt, higher density, all else equal.
glossary.observation: NASA Aquarius surface-salinity composite, August–September 2011. Colours show salt concentration; black marks missing data. This early product contains calibration artefacts and is not a map of deep-water salinity.

glossary.def: Transport in short hops or bounces, especially of sand grains moved by wind or flowing water.
glossary.observation: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind transports loose sand by surface creep and saltation; the dunes record accumulated transport rather than individual grain paths.

glossary.def: Soil mineral particles 0.05–2 mm across in the USDA system. Other sediment classifications use a slightly different lower boundary.
glossary.observation: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind transports loose sand by surface creep and saltation; the dunes record accumulated transport rather than individual grain paths.

glossary.def: A change between views representing very different sizes or distances. Each view needs its own scale because a single display cannot resolve all of them.
glossary.observation: NASA/ESA Hubble mosaic of Andromeda. Resolved stars and dust lanes provide an observed view of a galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away.

glossary.def: Daytime onshore flow driven by land heating faster than the sea.
glossary.observation: Aqua MODIS, 9 April 2013. Sea-breeze air moves inland and helps cumulus clouds develop over the warmer island. Silvery water is sunglint. This daytime image shows sea-breeze effects, not a night-time land breeze.

glossary.def: New oceanic crust at a ridge. Ocean floor is plate too, born and later destroyed.
glossary.observation: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading centre, where new oceanic crust is built.

glossary.def: An underwater mountain, usually volcanic. Seamounts need not lie on an age-progressive hotspot chain or have once stood above sea level.
glossary.observation: NOAA multibeam survey of an Arctic seamount. A seamount is a submarine mountain; a guyot is the flat-topped subtype. Surveyed topography, rather than colour alone, is needed to distinguish them.

glossary.def: Supply, transport, deposition, interruption. The whole-coast accounts.
glossary.observation: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore transport supplies a spit at the Humber estuary.

glossary.def: Rock from deposited fragments or precipitates, then lithified.
glossary.observation: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

glossary.def: A tidal pattern with two high waters and two low waters in each lunar day, which averages about 24 hours 50 minutes.
glossary.observation: Low tide at Waterford on St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The exposed harbour floor makes tidal range visible.

glossary.def: The failure plane. Curved in a slump. Not a vertical cliff face.
glossary.observation: Oso, Washington, 2014: an aerial photograph of the landslide source, travel path and deposit. The displaced material crossed the valley floor.

glossary.def: Shallow seafloor beside a continent. It lets a surge stand up.
glossary.observation: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Colour represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

glossary.def: Comparison of continental margins, rather than modern coastlines, when reconstructing former continental positions. Sediment cover and deformation make the fit approximate.
glossary.observation: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Colour represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

glossary.def: A broad volcano with gentle slopes built mainly by fluid lava flows, commonly basaltic. Mauna Loa is a classic example.
glossary.observation: Hawaii from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

glossary.def: The change in a wave as it enters shallower water: it slows, its wavelength shortens, and its height may increase before breaking.
glossary.observation: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

glossary.def: Solar radiation: ultraviolet, visible, near-infrared.
glossary.observation: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Colours show sunlight reflected by the Earth system in W m⁻². This is outgoing shortwave flux, not incoming solar irradiance or albedo itself.

glossary.def: Time to face the same star again: about 23 h 56 min. Shorter than the solar day because Earth also orbits.
glossary.observation: South Africa at night, photographed from the ISS. Earth's rotation relative to the Sun defines the solar day; rotation relative to distant stars defines the slightly shorter sidereal day.

glossary.def: Soil mineral particles 0.002–0.05 mm across in the USDA system, intermediate between clay and sand.
glossary.observation: NASA Landsat observation of the Thames estuary. The tidal river widens towards the North Sea; pale water reveals suspended material and shallow coastal water.

glossary.def: Locates a 100 m square on the OS grid. Not a pin.
glossary.observation: Ordnance Survey sheet NO, northeast Scotland. British National Grid eastings and northings are measured from a false origin southwest of Great Britain. Four figures identify a 1 km square; six identify a 100 m square. This reduced 1:250,000 sheet illustrates the system; use a detailed map for precise references.

glossary.def: Deposition on the inner bend of a meander.
glossary.observation: Ucayali River, Peru, photographed from the ISS. Meander migration leaves cut-offs and abandoned channels across the floodplain.

glossary.def: Carbon transfer through rocks, sediments and the deep Earth, involving weathering, burial, metamorphism and volcanism over geological timescales.
glossary.observation: Layered rocks at Grand Canyon record the geological carbon cycle and deep time. Lithification converts sediment into rock; the canyon also exposes much older basement in its inner gorge. A landscape photograph alone does not date individual beds.

glossary.def: Stored winter snow becoming spring discharge. A nival bump.
glossary.observation: Snowmelt near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. Seasonal melting transfers stored snow water into streams, soils and groundwater.

glossary.def: Angle of the Sun above the horizon. Noon altitude is the day’s peak.
glossary.observation: A working sundial at Green's Windmill, Nottingham. A gnomon's shadow connects the Sun's apparent direction with local solar time.

glossary.def: Total solar irradiance near Earth's mean orbital distance, about 1,361 W m⁻² on a surface perpendicular to the rays above the atmosphere. It varies slightly over time.
glossary.observation: NASA SDO observes the solar photosphere and sunspots. The Sun supplies incoming solar radiation (insolation). The solar constant is irradiance near 1 AU on a plane perpendicular to the rays, about 1,361 W m⁻²; it is not measured by this visible-light photograph.

glossary.def: Noon to noon. About 24 hours. The school-clock day.
glossary.observation: South Africa at night, photographed from the ISS. Earth's rotation relative to the Sun defines the solar day; rotation relative to distant stars defines the slightly shorter sidereal day.

glossary.def: An eclipse near new Moon when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun close to an orbital node. The apparent sizes determine whether it is total, annular or partial.
glossary.observation: NASA's airborne view of the 21 August 2017 total solar eclipse. The Moon blocks the bright photosphere, revealing the corona.

glossary.def: When one hemisphere leans most toward the Sun (June, NH) or most away (December, NH).
glossary.observation: Meteosat-9 observed this day–night boundary on 21 December 2010. Earth's tilted axis puts the subsolar point south of the equator and gives southern latitudes longer days. Declination is the Sun's angle north or south of the equatorial plane; the tilt of the boundary is observational evidence, not an angle scale.

glossary.def: Where channelised flow begins — a spring, a gathering of rills, or a lake outlet.
glossary.observation: Snowmelt near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. Seasonal melting transfers stored snow water into streams, soils and groundwater.

glossary.def: An elongated deposit of sand or shingle attached to land at one end and extending into water, commonly built by longshore sediment transport.
glossary.observation: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore transport supplies a spit at the Humber estuary.

glossary.def: A surveyed point with a printed elevation.
glossary.observation: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

glossary.def: How fast plates separate at a ridge. Centimetres per year, not a weather story.
glossary.observation: NOAA EMAG2 v3 maps measured magnetic anomalies. Ocean-floor bands record crust formed under changing magnetic polarity. Matching the pattern to dated reversals supports seafloor spreading and allows a rate to be calculated from distance divided by age; colour alone does not give rock age.

glossary.def: Where the water table meets the hillside and water emerges.
glossary.observation: Groundwater emerges at a karst spring in Alabama. Water stored in connected pores and fractures can return to the surface as spring flow.

glossary.def: Larger range. Sun and Moon pull along one line. New or full. Twice a month, not the season.
glossary.observation: Low water at St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. Tidal range changes through the spring–neap cycle as lunar and solar tidal effects combine. This single low-tide photograph does not establish whether it was a spring or neap tide.

glossary.def: A ridge of high ground. Contours V downhill.
glossary.observation: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

glossary.def: A narrow, often violent band of convection, commonly along or ahead of a cold front.
glossary.observation: A cold front passes Brock University, St. Catharines, Canada. The cloud edge makes uplift visible; the front itself is a zone of contrasting air.

glossary.def: An isolated pillar of coastal rock left by erosion and cliff retreat, sometimes after the collapse of a sea arch. Old Harry is chalk; Durdle Door is an arch in limestone.
glossary.observation: Hvítserkur, Iceland. This isolated coastal rock illustrates a stack, with openings cut through its base.

glossary.def: Height of the water surface. Not the same as discharge.
glossary.observation: USGS gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica, 12 December 2001. Repeated measurements of stage and discharge produce a river's hydrograph.

glossary.def: Dripstone growing down from a cave roof, if the drip has time.
glossary.observation: Stalactites in a cave on Mount Kyllini. Dissolved calcium carbonate is deposited as water drips and loses carbon dioxide.

glossary.def: Flooding described by the water level after short-period surface waves are averaged out. Coastal still-water level can include the tide and storm surge.
glossary.observation: The South Fork Stillaguamish River in flood. Water spreads beyond the usual channel when discharge exceeds channel capacity.

glossary.def: A place water sits: ocean, ice, aquifer, lake, soil, air.
glossary.observation: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon: living vegetation is a carbon store, exchanging carbon with the air and soil.

glossary.def: Sea-level rise from wind pile-up and low pressure. Not a tsunami.
glossary.observation: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

glossary.def: Layer above the tropopause, heated by ozone absorbing ultraviolet.
glossary.observation: Earth's thin atmosphere above the limb, photographed from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight reveals lower atmospheric layers; coloured bands are not precise altitude boundaries.

glossary.def: A commonly steep-sided volcano built from successive lava flows and fragmental deposits. Its magma composition and eruption style can vary; many form above subduction zones.
glossary.observation: Mount Fuji from Lake Kawaguchi, Japan. Repeated eruptions built a stratovolcano with layers of lava and fragmental deposits.

glossary.def: Fault movement that is mainly horizontal and parallel to the fault's strike. Some strike-slip faults form plate-transform boundaries; others lie within plates.
glossary.observation: San Andreas Fault in California's Sierra Madre Mountains. The fault accommodates mainly horizontal motion between the Pacific and North American plates.

glossary.def: What remains in the surf after a stack fails.
glossary.observation: The Pinnacles coast, Purbeck, Dorset. Erosion leaves isolated stacks and lower remnants called stumps beside the retreating chalk cliffs.

glossary.def: The descent of one lithospheric plate beneath another into the mantle at a convergent boundary, commonly involving oceanic lithosphere.
glossary.observation: NASA ARIA observations of surface displacement following the 2025 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake. The coloured displacement field is measured evidence of movement, not a photograph of the buried fault.

glossary.def: Belt of sinking air on the poleward side of Hadley. Deserts often sit under it.
glossary.observation: GOES-East cloud observations over the Americas, 22 April 2014. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude systems provide evidence of atmospheric circulation. The three-cell pattern is a long-term zonal average, not three fixed cloud rings in this single image.

glossary.def: The day’s arc on the sky dome. Date and latitude write it.
glossary.observation: A working sundial at Green's Windmill, Nottingham. A gnomon's shadow connects the Sun's apparent direction with local solar time.

glossary.def: A relatively cool, dark region of the solar photosphere associated with strong magnetic fields.
glossary.observation: NASA SDO observation of active region AR 12192 in 2014. Sunspots are cooler areas of the photosphere; the orange display colour is image processing.

glossary.def: An assembly of most continents. Pangaea is one of several in Earth history.
glossary.observation: Permian Glossopteris leaf from Antarctica. Related fossils on separated southern continents are evidence that these lands were once joined within Gondwana, which formed part of Pangaea.

glossary.def: Flow in the upper ocean, driven by winds and pressure gradients and modified by rotation, coastlines and mixing.
glossary.observation: MODIS, 2 May 2001: thermal contrast traces the Gulf Stream and eddies. Brightness temperature includes the sea surface and overlying moist atmosphere.

glossary.def: Where the sloping front meets the ground. The line on the chart.
glossary.observation: Cloud accompanying a cold front at Brock University, Ontario. A surface front is where the sloping boundary between air masses meets the ground. The visible cloud edge does not locate that intersection precisely.

glossary.def: Love and Rayleigh waves along the free surface. Often the damage in town.
glossary.observation: USGS seismometer installation in Puerto Rico. Wave arrival times and recorded ground motion are used to estimate an earthquake's focus, epicentre and magnitude; none of those buried locations is visible in this photograph.

glossary.def: Transport of fine sediment within moving water or air, kept aloft by turbulence rather than continuously resting on the bed or ground.
glossary.observation: NASA Landsat observation of the Thames estuary. The tidal river widens towards the North Sea; pale water reveals suspended material and shallow coastal water.

glossary.def: An opening where a surface stream enters underground drainage, usually in karst. A doline or sinkhole is a depression and need not contain a sinking stream.
glossary.observation: Stream Passage Pot, Ingleborough, North Yorkshire. This entrance belongs to the Gaping Gill karst drainage system, where surface water enters underground passages.

glossary.def: A fold with the youngest rocks in its core. In a simple upright syncline, layers dip towards the centre; erosion can leave either a ridge or valley above it.
glossary.observation: Folded strata at The Settlands, Wales. Trace a bed through the exposure to see deformation recorded in solid rock.

glossary.def: New Moon to new Moon: about 29.53 days.
glossary.observation: The Moon's sunlit crescent photographed from Artemis II. A synodic month is the interval between matching lunar phases, about 29.5 days; one photograph records only one moment in that cycle.

glossary.def: Sun, Moon, and Earth in one line. Spring tide. Exam word for the alignment.
glossary.observation: NASA's airborne view of the 21 August 2017 total solar eclipse. The Moon blocks the bright photosphere, revealing the corona.

glossary.def: A statistical relationship between climate or weather variations in distant regions, such as the influence of ENSO on rainfall probabilities.
glossary.observation: Sentinel-6 mapped sea-surface height anomalies during La Niña in January 2025. Ocean–atmosphere coupling changes the Walker circulation and can influence distant weather through teleconnections; these atmospheric links are not directly pictured.

glossary.def: The boundary between the illuminated and dark hemispheres of a planet or moon. Earth's rotation carries places across it; changing solar declination alters its seasonal orientation.
glossary.observation: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 20 March 2011. The terminator passes close to both poles around the equinox; refraction and the Sun's finite disc mean observed daylight is not exactly twelve hours everywhere.

glossary.def: The boundary between Earth's illuminated and dark hemispheres. Its position changes with time of day and with the Sun's seasonal declination.
glossary.observation: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 20 March 2011. The terminator passes close to both poles around the equinox; refraction and the Sun's finite disc mean observed daylight is not exactly twelve hours everywhere.

glossary.def: Three components that must sum to 100 percent. Silt is the remainder here.
glossary.observation: NPS scientists examine soil texture in the field. Sand, silt and clay proportions can be plotted on a ternary texture triangle; the photograph shows the sampled material and fieldwork.

glossary.def: A body of crust with a geological history distinct from neighbouring regions, often joined to a continent by tectonic accretion.
glossary.observation: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag juxtaposes rocks with different geological histories. Such field contacts help reconstruct the Caledonian mountain belt and its crustal terranes; boundaries between terranes need regional evidence as well as one outcrop.

glossary.def: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars: rock and metal, close in.
glossary.observation: Apollo 17's Blue Marble, 7 December 1972. Earth's axial tilt changes the angle and duration of sunlight over the year.

glossary.def: The sand, silt and clay proportions of the mineral soil.
glossary.observation: NPS scientists examine soil texture in the field. Sand, silt and clay proportions can be plotted on a ternary texture triangle; the photograph shows the sampled material and fieldwork.

glossary.def: A loop driven by uneven heating and the pressure difference that follows.
glossary.observation: Cloud streets over the Bering Sea, 20 January 2006. Cold air over warmer water supports convection organised into rolls by the wind.

glossary.def: A belt of the highest mean temperatures at a given season. It shifts with seasonal heating and geography and does not always coincide with the geographic equator or ITCZ.
glossary.observation: GOES-East cloud observations over the Americas, 22 April 2014. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude systems provide evidence of atmospheric circulation. The three-cell pattern is a long-term zonal average, not three fixed cloud rings in this single image.

glossary.def: Relating to seawater density differences caused by temperature and salinity. These contribute to ocean overturning alongside wind forcing and mixing.
glossary.observation: NOAA CTD water sampling. Temperature and salinity observations constrain water density and help identify deep-water masses such as North Atlantic Deep Water. The instrument photo does not show the global circulation itself.

glossary.def: The very thin atmospheric layer above roughly 85 km where kinetic temperature generally rises with altitude as gases absorb energetic solar radiation. Much auroral activity occurs here.
glossary.observation: An ISS photograph of aurora north of Antarctica. Energetic particles excite upper-atmosphere gases; the green light is emitted by the atmosphere, not reflected sunlight.

glossary.def: An idealised elevation of the ocean surface in an equilibrium-tide model. Real tides are moving waves modified by basin shape, depth, rotation and coastlines.
glossary.observation: Low water at St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. Tidal range changes through the spring–neap cycle as lunar and solar tidal effects combine. This single low-tide photograph does not establish whether it was a spring or neap tide.

glossary.def: High water minus low water. Springs large, neaps small. Coasts then reshape the number.
glossary.observation: Low tide at Waterford on St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The exposed harbour floor makes tidal range visible.

glossary.def: Sediment deposited directly by glacier ice, usually containing an unsorted mixture of particle sizes.
glossary.observation: A natural exposure of glacial till. Ice deposits a mixture of grain sizes directly, often without the sorting produced by flowing water.

glossary.def: A region using an agreed standard civil time. Boundaries follow political and practical choices and are not necessarily 15° wide.
glossary.observation: South African cities at night from the ISS. Earth's rotation underlies the daily cycle; civil time zones and the International Date Line are agreed conventions, not visible lines on Earth's surface.

glossary.def: The downslope bulge. On a coast, waves pick it apart.
glossary.observation: Oso, Washington, 2014: an aerial photograph of the landslide source, travel path and deposit. The displaced material crossed the valley floor.

glossary.def: A ridge of deposited sand or shingle connecting an island to the mainland or another island, often formed where wave refraction favours deposition.
glossary.observation: Giens, near Hyères, France. The double tombolo connects the peninsula to the mainland through two sediment-built barriers.

glossary.def: A reference level above most atmospheric absorption and scattering, used when describing incoming and outgoing radiation. Solar irradiance also needs a specified distance and surface orientation.
glossary.observation: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Colours show sunlight reflected by the Earth system in W m⁻². This is outgoing shortwave flux, not incoming solar irradiance or albedo itself.

glossary.def: Surface return of the Hadley cell, toward the ITCZ, deflected by Coriolis.
glossary.observation: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favour wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

glossary.def: A flow between stores.
glossary.observation: Snowmelt near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. Seasonal melting transfers stored snow water into streams, soils and groundwater.

glossary.def: Plates slide past. Strike-slip faults.
glossary.observation: San Andreas Fault in California's Sierra Madre Mountains. The fault accommodates mainly horizontal motion between the Pacific and North American plates.

glossary.def: A long, narrow depression in the seafloor associated with a subduction zone, where an oceanic plate bends down towards the mantle.
glossary.observation: NOAA bathymetric visualisation of the Puerto Rico region. A trench is an elongated seafloor depression associated here with a complex convergent plate boundary; vertical relief is exaggerated in this perspective.

glossary.def: A stream that joins a larger channel.
glossary.observation: ASTER, 24 September 2005: tributaries dissect sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. A drainage network collects flow towards a main river.

glossary.def: Warm-core organised storm over a warm ocean. Name depends on basin.
glossary.observation: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

glossary.def: 23.44°N to 23.44°S. Overhead Sun lives only in this belt, and not every day.
glossary.observation: NASA Blue Marble monthly composite in an equirectangular latitude–longitude grid. Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the equator; parallels run east–west. The geographic reference lines are mathematical, not marks on the land.

glossary.def: The boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere, identified mainly by a change in the vertical temperature gradient. Its altitude varies with latitude and weather.
glossary.observation: Earth's thin atmosphere above the limb, photographed from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight reveals lower atmospheric layers; coloured bands are not precise altitude boundaries.

glossary.def: The lowest atmospheric layer, containing most air mass and nearly all weather. It is typically about 8 km deep near the poles and 16–18 km near the tropics.
glossary.observation: Earth's thin atmosphere above the limb, photographed from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight reveals lower atmospheric layers; coloured bands are not precise altitude boundaries.

glossary.def: A view in which stated lengths use the same scale factor. If a display still exaggerates a feature or compresses distances, it must identify that exception explicitly.
glossary.observation: Cassini photographed Saturn and its rings together. Their apparent proportions belong to one perspective view; a true-scale model must use the same length multiplier for every dimension, with foreshortening treated separately.

glossary.def: Long-period wave from a sudden water displacement, often seafloor slip.
glossary.observation: Coastal damage after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. Run-up is the maximum vertical elevation reached by the water above a reference sea level; survey evidence is needed to attach a number to this photograph.

glossary.def: Wide floor and steep walls overdeepened by ice.
glossary.observation: Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Flowing ice carries debris; its dark medial moraines record where tributary glaciers join.

glossary.def: The dark core of a shadow. A total lunar eclipse puts the Moon in Earth’s umbra.
glossary.observation: NASA's airborne view of the 21 August 2017 total solar eclipse. The Moon blocks the bright photosphere, revealing the corona.

glossary.def: The movement of deeper water towards the surface, often driven by winds that move surface water away or by large-scale ocean circulation.
glossary.observation: Aqua MODIS, 5 May 2020. Upwelling in the Canary Current system supplies nutrients off Mauritania. The visible green water contains phytoplankton and sediment; it is not a temperature map.

glossary.def: An urban area that is warmer than nearby surroundings, often most evident at night. Surface materials, reduced evaporation, urban geometry and waste heat contribute.
glossary.observation: ECOSTRESS measured London's land-surface temperatures near midnight on 15 July 2022. Built surfaces remained warmer than many vegetated areas. These are surface temperatures, not standard air-temperature readings.

glossary.def: Ternary chart that names a class from sand, silt and clay percentages.
glossary.observation: NPS scientists examine soil texture in the field. Sand, silt and clay proportions can be plotted on a ternary texture triangle; the photograph shows the sampled material and fieldwork.

glossary.def: Cross-profile of upland fluvial vertical erosion. Ice makes U.
glossary.observation: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

glossary.def: Low ground, often with a stream. Contours V uphill.
glossary.observation: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District, England. A landscape photograph shows local relief, ridges and valley slopes.

glossary.def: Magnetic stripes as a tape recorder of reversals and spreading.
glossary.observation: NOAA EMAG2 v3 maps measured magnetic anomalies. Ocean-floor bands record crust formed under changing magnetic polarity. Matching the pattern to dated reversals supports seafloor spreading and allows a rate to be calculated from distance divided by age; colour alone does not give rock age.

glossary.def: Resistance to flow. High viscosity plus gas makes explosive eruptions more likely.
glossary.observation: Kīlauea, 25 February 1983. USGS photographed a lava fountain approximately 10 metres high; molten rock is at the surface, not throughout the mantle.

glossary.def: Zonal tropical Pacific circulation. Neutral: rise west, sink east.
glossary.observation: Sentinel-6 mapped sea-surface height anomalies during La Niña in January 2025. Ocean–atmosphere coupling changes the Walker circulation and can influence distant weather through teleconnections; these atmospheric links are not directly pictured.

glossary.def: Leading edge of warmer air. Gentler slope. Cloud thickening ahead.
glossary.observation: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

glossary.def: A region of unusually warm tropical surface water. In the Pacific, its extent and position change with winds and ENSO.
glossary.observation: AMSR-E, 19 October 2004. This warm-pool region was cooler than its long-term average. Colours show temperature anomalies, not absolute water temperature; a negative anomaly does not mean the water is cold in absolute terms.

glossary.def: The milder air between the warm front and the cold front in a midlatitude cyclone.
glossary.observation: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

glossary.def: Top of the saturated zone. A surface through the pores, not a lake shore.
glossary.observation: USGS observation well in Stephen C. Foster State Park, Georgia. Instruments record groundwater levels; the water table itself lies beneath the surface.

glossary.def: In UK geography, the drainage divide separating basins. In US usage, watershed commonly means the entire drainage basin; check the context.
glossary.observation: ASTER, 24 September 2005: tributaries dissect sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. A drainage network collects flow towards a main river.

glossary.def: Crest to crest. A tsunami’s is huge in deep water.
glossary.observation: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

glossary.def: Physical breakdown or chemical alteration of rock at or near Earth's surface, without transporting the material away. Chemical weathering also participates in the carbon cycle.
glossary.observation: Weathered granite documented by GeoDIL. Mineral breakdown and disintegration progressively turn intact rock into weathered material.

glossary.def: Breakdown that feeds the sedimentary path. Not the same as erosion.
glossary.observation: Weathered granite documented by GeoDIL. Mineral breakdown and disintegration progressively turn intact rock into weathered material.

glossary.def: Midlatitude west-to-east winds. The UK’s usual steering, under the Ferrel story.
glossary.observation: GOES-East cloud observations over the Americas, 22 April 2014. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude systems provide evidence of atmospheric circulation. The three-cell pattern is a long-term zonal average, not three fixed cloud rings in this single image.

glossary.def: Narrow, fast, warm current on the western side of a subtropical gyre — Gulf Stream, Kuroshio.
glossary.observation: MODIS, 2 May 2001: thermal contrast traces the Gulf Stream and eddies. Brightness temperature includes the sea surface and overlying moist atmosphere.

glossary.def: A global geodetic reference system used by GPS, including a reference ellipsoid and coordinate frame. Converting to the British National Grid requires a projection and datum transformation.
glossary.observation: The historic Greenwich Meridian makes a reference longitude tangible. Modern WGS84 zero longitude lies about 102 metres east of this line.

glossary.def: The opening and closing of ocean basins, named for Tuzo Wilson.
glossary.observation: The East African Rift in Kenya: continental extension is an opening stage of a possible ocean-basin cycle. A rift does not inevitably become an ocean.

glossary.def: A dry col on the old course, left after capture.
glossary.observation: Bald Eagle Mountain, Pennsylvania. The wind gap crossed by Route 15 is left of centre; Hagermans Run occupies a separate water gap to the right. A wind gap lacks the through-flowing river found in a water gap.

glossary.def: The slope of the sea surface forced by wind stress.
glossary.observation: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

glossary.def: The upslope side that faces the incoming moist air.
glossary.observation: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favour wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

glossary.def: Streamlined wind-eroded ridge, wind-parallel. Carved.
glossary.observation: Yardangs at Dunhuang, China. Persistent wind erosion shapes elongated ridges in relatively soft rock or sediment.

labs.title: Why seasons happen
labs.hook: Earth’s tilted axis changes the angle of sunlight and the length of the day as Earth travels around the Sun.
labs.objective: Explain seasons using axial tilt, not distance from the Sun, and predict which hemisphere is in summer on a given date.
curriculum: APES 4.7 Solar radiation and Earth’s seasons

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Keep Orbit stretch at 0 and set Axial tilt to 0°. Play a year and read the two 12-hour daylight values. Switch to Earth close-up to inspect the terminator and axis.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set tilt to 23.44° and pause at the June direction, then December. Compare London with Sydney and trace the fixed axis direction.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain what changed and why. The adjustable orbit is an experiment for isolating tilt and distance; its calendar alignment is not Earth’s actual orbit.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: What would happen to seasons if axial tilt were 0°?
choices: Seasons would reverse: June would be winter in London.
Almost no seasons: day length and noon Sun height would stay nearly constant at each latitude.
Seasons would get stronger because the orbit would become more elliptical.
The equator would freeze and the poles would heat up.
questions.explain: With no tilt, every latitude keeps a nearly fixed day length and solar altitude. The small remaining change is orbital eccentricity, which is not what we mean by seasons.

questions.prompt: Why is December summer in Sydney?
choices: Australia is closer to the Sun in December.
The southern hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun in December.
The Moon pulls the southern oceans toward the Sun.
questions.explain: In December the South Pole leans toward the Sun. Sydney gets higher noon Sun and longer days. London gets the opposite.

questions.prompt: Earth is slightly nearer the Sun in early January. Does that cause northern winter?
choices: Yes — closer means colder because of faster orbit.
No. Perihelion is in January, but northern winter is a tilt effect. The southern hemisphere is in summer then.
No, because January is actually aphelion.
questions.explain: Near perihelion the solar input is about 3.4% above the 1 AU value, and about 6.9% greater than at aphelion. Both hemispheres receive that distance effect together; their opposite seasons primarily reflect tilt.

questions.prompt: At the equator, how do day length and solar altitude change through the year compared with London?
choices: The equator has polar night in June.
Day length stays near 12 hours; noon Sun stays high, shifting only with the 23.44° declination. London’s day length swings from about 8 to 16 hours.
They change the same way; only temperature differs.
The equator has no noon Sun in December.
questions.explain: Equatorial day length is always close to 12 hours. Solar altitude stays high. Mid-latitude places like London swing hard in both day length and noon altitude.

why: Earth’s tilted axis changes the angle of sunlight and the length of the day as Earth travels around the Sun. When one hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, the other experiences winter.
Set tilt to 23.44° and pause at the June direction, then December. Compare London with Sydney and trace the fixed axis direction.
The adjustable orbit is an experiment for isolating tilt and distance; its calendar alignment is not Earth’s actual orbit.

glossary.def: The angle between a body's rotation axis and the perpendicular to its orbital plane. Earth's tilt is about 23.44°, and its axis keeps nearly the same direction over one orbit.
The boundary between the illuminated and dark hemispheres of a planet or moon. Earth's rotation carries places across it; changing solar declination alters its seasonal orientation.
When one hemisphere leans most toward the Sun (June, NH) or most away (December, NH).
The instant when the Sun crosses Earth's equatorial plane. Daylight is close to twelve hours around this date, but the Sun's disc, refraction and latitude affect observed day length.
The latitude where the Sun is overhead at noon. It travels between 23.44°N and 23.44°S.
Nearest point to the Sun. Early January. A few percent extra insolation, not the cause of seasons.
One trip around the Sun. About 365.25 days. Not the same as rotation (the daily spin).

misconception.claim: Summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.
misconception.truth: Seasons are a tilt effect. Earth is actually nearest the Sun in early January, during northern winter.

misconceptions.claim: Summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.
misconceptions.truth: Seasons are a tilt effect. Earth is actually nearest the Sun in early January, during northern winter.

misconceptions.claim: The axis wobbles each year, pointing first north then south.
misconceptions.truth: Over one year the axis stays pointed the same way, near Polaris. The hemisphere that leans toward the Sun changes because Earth has moved around the orbit.

misconceptions.claim: The equator has no seasons, so the Sun is always overhead there.
misconceptions.truth: Equatorial day length stays near 12 hours, but noon altitude still shifts with declination. Overhead Sun only happens between the tropics, and not every day.

teacher.script:
Begin with the model paused. Keep Orbit stretch at 0 and set Axial tilt to 0°. Play a year and read the two 12-hour daylight values. Switch to Earth close-up to inspect the terminator and axis.

Ask students to predict the result before changing a control. Set tilt to 23.44° and pause at the June direction, then December. Compare London with Sydney and trace the fixed axis direction.

Invite a student or geography club member to explain the comparison using the terms in this lab. The adjustable orbit is an experiment for isolating tilt and distance; its calendar alignment is not Earth’s actual orbit. Finish with a question from Check and ask for the evidence behind each answer.
pitfalls: Reading model-year progress as a precise calendar date.
Calling seasonal illumination a temperature forecast.
Treating an enlarged Earth or axis as the orbit-distance scale.

modelNotes: Orbit stretch changes a hypothetical eccentricity from 0 to 0.4.
Earth’s actual eccentricity is about 0.0167 and its perihelion is in early January; that calendar alignment is not represented by this March-origin experiment.
Set tilt to zero and circular orbit to compare 12-hour days outside the exact poles.

labs.title: Earth rotation and the terminator
labs.hook: Earth turns eastward, carrying each location into sunlight and then darkness.
labs.objective: State that Earth rotates west to east, that 15° of longitude is one hour, and that time zones are a consequence of rotation, not the cause of day and night.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Watch Earth turn west to east, carrying places into daylight and then darkness. Compare London, Cairo, Nairobi and Sydney.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Pause and drag the hour slider. One hour is 15° of longitude. Toggle the time-zone bands. They follow the spin; they do not cause it.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain what changed and why. The time-zone bands divide longitude into ideal 15° intervals; actual civil time zones follow local decisions and borders.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Which way does Earth rotate, viewed from above the North Pole?
choices: It does not rotate; the Sun orbits Earth.
questions.explain: West to east. That is why the Sun appears to rise in the east.

questions.prompt: Why is 15° of longitude equal to one hour?
choices: 360° / 24 h = 15° per hour. Time zones were drawn to match that geometry.
It is a coincidence of the metric system.
questions.explain: A full turn is 360° in 24 solar hours. Time zones are a human overlay on that arithmetic.

questions.prompt: What is the common misconception this lab targets?
choices: That the Sun moves around Earth each day.
Both the Sun-around-Earth idea and the idea that time zones cause day and night.
questions.explain: Day and night are the planet turning. Time zones are a civil convenience on top.

questions.prompt: If it is noon in London, about what local solar time is it in Cairo (~30°E)?
choices: The same, because they share a continent.
questions.explain: 30° / 15° per hour = 2 hours. East is later in the day.

why: Earth turns eastward, carrying each location into sunlight and then darkness. The boundary between day and night is called the terminator; it separates the illuminated and unilluminated halves of Earth.
Pause and drag the hour slider. One hour is 15° of longitude. Toggle the time-zone bands. They follow the spin; they do not cause it.
The time-zone bands divide longitude into ideal 15° intervals; actual civil time zones follow local decisions and borders.

glossary.def: Earth spinning on its axis. One solar day ≈ 24 hours.
The boundary between the illuminated and dark hemispheres of a planet or moon. Earth's rotation carries places across it; changing solar declination alters its seasonal orientation.
A line of longitude. Local solar noon is when the Sun crosses your meridian.
A region using an agreed standard civil time. Boundaries follow political and practical choices and are not necessarily 15° wide.
Time to face the same star again: about 23 h 56 min. Shorter than the solar day because Earth also orbits.
Noon to noon. About 24 hours. The school-clock day.

misconception.claim: The Sun moves around Earth once a day.
misconception.truth: Earth rotates west to east. The Sun only appears to move.

misconceptions.claim: The Sun moves around Earth once a day.
misconceptions.truth: Earth rotates west to east. The Sun only appears to move.

misconceptions.claim: Time zones cause day and night.
misconceptions.truth: Zones are civil labels on meridians. Day and night are which face of the planet sees the Sun.

misconceptions.claim: A 24-hour day is the time Earth takes to face the same star again.
misconceptions.truth: That is the sidereal day, about 23 h 56 min. The solar day is 24 h because Earth has also moved along its orbit.

teacher.script:
Begin with the model paused. Watch Earth turn west to east, carrying places into daylight and then darkness. Compare London, Cairo, Nairobi and Sydney.

Ask students to predict the result before changing a control. Pause and drag the hour slider. One hour is 15° of longitude. Toggle the time-zone bands. They follow the spin; they do not cause it.

Invite a student or geography club member to explain the comparison using the terms in this lab. The time-zone bands divide longitude into ideal 15° intervals; actual civil time zones follow local decisions and borders. Finish with a question from Check and ask for the evidence behind each answer.
pitfalls: Globe animations that rotate the wrong way (east to west).
Calling 24 h the sidereal day.

modelNotes: A Leeds frost at 07:00 is already sunlight on a Berlin school roof.
What is conserved: 360° in about 24 hours relative to the Sun, 15° per school hour.
Sidereal day is about 23 h 56 min; solar day is 24 h.

labs.title: Moon phases and Sun–Earth–Moon geometry
labs.hook: Sunlight illuminates half the Moon.
labs.objective: Link each phase to the Moon’s position around Earth, distinguish the synodic month from a single night, and show why eclipses are rare.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Play a synodic month. Watch the lit half of the Moon always face the Sun, while the face we see from Earth changes.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Pause at first quarter and full. Toggle the Earth-view disc. Then turn on eclipse alignment: the 5° orbital tilt is why most months have no eclipse.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain what changed and why. Sizes and separations are enlarged for inspection; compare physical scale to see how widely separated Earth and Moon really are.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: At first quarter, where is the Moon relative to the Sun and Earth?
choices: About 90° around its orbit from the Sun–Earth line.
questions.explain: We see half the near side lit. That is a right angle in the Sun–Earth–Moon triangle.

questions.prompt: Does Earth’s shadow cause the ordinary crescent Moon?
choices: No. The dark part is the Moon’s own night side. Earth’s shadow is a lunar eclipse, and it is rare.
questions.explain: Phases depend on the visible illuminated fraction. Eclipses require alignment near an orbital node; the orbit itself remains tilted by about 5°.

questions.prompt: Why are eclipses rarer than full and new Moons?
choices: The Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5° to the ecliptic, so it usually passes above or below Earth’s shadow.
questions.explain: New and full happen every synodic month. Eclipses need the Moon near a node.

questions.prompt: A synodic month is about 29.5 days. What is it measuring?
choices: The time from new Moon to new Moon as seen from Earth.
The time for the Moon to rotate once.
questions.explain: The Moon also has to catch up with Earth’s motion around the Sun, so the synodic month is longer than the sidereal month (~27.3 days).

why: Sunlight illuminates half the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different proportions of that illuminated half, producing the phases; Earth’s shadow is involved only in a lunar eclipse.
Pause at first quarter and full. Toggle the Earth-view disc. Then turn on eclipse alignment: the 5° orbital tilt is why most months have no eclipse.
Sizes and separations are enlarged for inspection; compare physical scale to see how widely separated Earth and Moon really are.

glossary.def: The fraction of the near side that is sunlit, as seen from Earth.
New Moon to new Moon: about 29.53 days.
The dark core of a shadow. A total lunar eclipse puts the Moon in Earth’s umbra.
The Moon’s orbit is tilted ~5° to Earth’s orbit. That is why eclipses are rare.
Where the Moon’s orbit crosses the ecliptic. Eclipses need the Moon near a node.
The plane of Earth’s orbit. The Moon is tilted about 5° to it.
The hemisphere of the Moon that usually faces Earth because the Moon rotates once per orbit. Libration lets us see somewhat more than half its surface over time.
The part of a shadow where the light source is only partly obscured. On the Moon it produces subtler dimming than the umbra.

misconception.claim: The crescent is Earth’s shadow on the Moon.
misconception.truth: The crescent is the Moon’s night side. Earth’s shadow is an eclipse.

misconceptions.claim: The crescent is Earth’s shadow on the Moon.
misconceptions.truth: The crescent is the Moon’s night side. Earth’s shadow is an eclipse.

misconceptions.claim: The Moon is only in the sky at night, and only when it is full.
misconceptions.truth: A first-quarter Moon is high in the afternoon. Phase is a viewing angle, not a schedule of appearance.

misconceptions.claim: Every full Moon is a lunar eclipse.
misconceptions.truth: The Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5°. Full happens every month; an eclipse needs the Moon near a node.

teacher.script:
Begin with the model paused. Play a synodic month. Watch the lit half of the Moon always face the Sun, while the face we see from Earth changes.

Ask students to predict the result before changing a control. Pause at first quarter and full. Toggle the Earth-view disc. Then turn on eclipse alignment: the 5° orbital tilt is why most months have no eclipse.

Invite a student or geography club member to explain the comparison using the terms in this lab. Sizes and separations are enlarged for inspection; compare physical scale to see how widely separated Earth and Moon really are. Finish with a question from Check and ask for the evidence behind each answer.
pitfalls: Ball-and-lamp demos that put the Moon in Earth’s shadow for a crescent.
Scale: the Moon is 30 Earth-diameters away. This lab exaggerates size so the geometry reads from the back of the room.

modelNotes: The Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5° to the ecliptic, so most months it misses Earth’s shadow.
Size here is exaggerated so the set reads from the back of the room; the real Moon is about 30 Earth-diameters away.
Synodic month, new to new, is about 29.53 days, longer than the sidereal month because Earth has moved.
Toggle eclipse alignment — the 5° tilt going to zero — and ask why next month’s full Moon will not be an eclipse.
Without the 3D view: half the Moon is always sunlit; phases are the viewing angle from Earth; eclipses need the Moon near a node of its tilted orbit.
A synodic month is new to new, about 29.5 days.

labs.title: Earth’s interior
labs.hook: Seismic waves reveal an Earth with layers that differ in composition and physical state.
labs.objective: Name the four main layers, their state, and why a liquid outer core plus P/S-wave shadows tell us the inside is not uniform rock.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Rotate the cutaway, then change Slice and Explode. Identify the four layers and read their material states.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Restore unexploded spacing, then enable P/S waves. Compare transmission through solid mantle and liquid outer core.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain what changed and why. The cutaway shows a reference structure; its illustrative wave paths explain transmission rather than calculating earthquake travel times.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: The outer core is liquid iron–nickel. The inner core is solid iron–nickel despite being hotter, because pressure is higher.

questions.prompt: Why is there a direct S-wave shadow on the far side of Earth?
choices: S-waves cannot travel through the liquid outer core, so a shadow covers the far side.
questions.explain: S-waves are shear. Liquids do not take a shear. That is the classic evidence for a liquid core.

questions.prompt: Why does a liquid outer core matter for the magnetic field?
choices: Moving conducting metal can sustain a geodynamo. A fully solid Earth would not.
questions.explain: The geodynamo needs a convecting, electrically conducting fluid. That is the outer core.

questions.prompt: About how thick is continental crust compared with Earth’s radius (~6371 km)?
choices: The same as the outer core.
questions.explain: Continental crust averages ~35 km; oceanic ~7 km. It is a skin, not a layer you could walk around inside.

why: Seismic waves reveal an Earth with layers that differ in composition and physical state. The mantle is mainly solid rock, the outer core is liquid, and the inner core is solid.
Restore unexploded spacing, then enable P/S waves. Compare transmission through solid mantle and liquid outer core.
The cutaway shows a reference structure; its illustrative wave paths explain transmission rather than calculating earthquake travel times.

glossary.def: Earth's outermost compositional layer of solid rock. Oceanic crust averages about 7 km thick; continental crust commonly spans roughly 30–70 km.
Solid but convecting silicate rock to ~2900 km. Most of Earth’s volume. Not a magma ocean.
Earth's liquid metallic layer, mainly iron with nickel and lighter elements, between about 2,890 and 5,150 km depth. It does not transmit shear waves.
Solid iron–nickel sphere ~1220 km in radius.
A compressional seismic wave with particle motion parallel to its travel direction. It travels through solids and liquids and is the faster body-wave type.
A shear seismic wave with particle motion perpendicular to its travel direction. It propagates through solids but not through the liquid outer core.
Crust plus the rigid top of the mantle. Plates are lithosphere, not crust alone.
The generation of Earth's magnetic field by motion of electrically conducting liquid metal in the outer core, influenced by Earth's rotation.

misconception.claim: The mantle is a sea of molten lava.
misconception.truth: The mantle is overwhelmingly solid. Magma is a local, partial melt. The liquid layer is the outer core, and it is metal, not lava.

misconceptions.claim: The mantle is a sea of molten lava.
misconceptions.truth: The mantle is overwhelmingly solid. Magma is a local, partial melt. The liquid layer is the outer core, and it is metal, not lava.

misconceptions.claim: We have samples from the core, like we have Moon rocks.
misconceptions.truth: We have not. The deepest borehole is crust. Core composition is inferred from seismology, density, and meteorite chemistry.

misconceptions.claim: The crust is a thick layer you could walk around inside.
misconceptions.truth: Continental crust averages about 35 km on a 6371 km radius. This lab draws it ×4 so you can see it. It is a film.

teacher.script:
Begin with the model paused. Rotate the cutaway, then change Slice and Explode. Identify the four layers and read their material states.

Ask students to predict the result before changing a control. Restore unexploded spacing, then enable P/S waves. Compare transmission through solid mantle and liquid outer core.

Invite a student or geography club member to explain the comparison using the terms in this lab. The cutaway shows a reference structure; its illustrative wave paths explain transmission rather than calculating earthquake travel times. Finish with a question from Check and ask for the evidence behind each answer.
pitfalls: Calling the mantle a magma ocean.
Treating the illustrative straight paths as a calculation of seismic shadow zones.
Comparing depths while layers are exploded.

modelNotes: This section uses a uniform 35 km reference crust, a core–mantle boundary at radius 3480 km and an inner-core radius of 1221 km.
Oceanic crust is commonly 5–10 km thick and continental crust commonly 30–50 km; real boundaries are not perfectly concentric spheres.

labs.title: Plate boundaries
labs.hook: At divergent boundaries plates separate, at convergent boundaries they approach, and at transform boundaries they slide past.
labs.objective: Distinguish divergent, convergent and transform boundaries, name a landform for each, and compare reconstructed continental positions through time.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Rotate the present-day globe. Teal marks divergent boundaries, coral convergent boundaries, and sand transform boundaries. Switch to Boundary section to compare their motion.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Scrub the globe back towards Pangaea using 10 Ma GPlates snapshots. These are modern coastlines carried by a plate-motion model, not ancient shorelines. Return to 0 Ma to locate Hawaii.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain what changed and why. Past views move modern coastlines using a plate model, so they show continental positions rather than ancient shorelines.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is which boundary type?
questions.explain: Plates move apart. New oceanic crust forms. Iceland sits on the ridge.
India collided with Eurasia. No ocean trench now — two continents stacked.

questions.prompt: The San Andreas Fault is famous because it is a…
choices: Transform boundary between the Pacific and North American plates.
questions.explain: Plates slide past. Big earthquakes, few volcanoes. Cascadia to the north is the subduction zone.

questions.prompt: A hotspot track like Hawaii is evidence that…
choices: A plate can move over a relatively fixed mantle plume, leaving a chain of volcanoes that get older away from the active island.
All volcanoes sit on mid-ocean ridges.
questions.explain: Loihi and Hawaiʻi are young; Emperor seamounts are old and to the northwest.

why: At divergent boundaries plates separate, at convergent boundaries they approach, and at transform boundaries they slide past. These relative motions help explain the distribution of ridges, trenches and earthquakes.
Scrub the globe back towards Pangaea using 10 Ma GPlates snapshots. These are modern coastlines carried by a plate-motion model, not ancient shorelines. Return to 0 Ma to locate Hawaii.
Past views move modern coastlines using a plate model, so they show continental positions rather than ancient shorelines.

glossary.def: Plates move apart. Mid-ocean ridge or continental rift.
Plates move together. Subduction or collision.
Plates slide past. Strike-slip faults.
A region of persistent volcanism that can occur within a plate or at a boundary. Many hotspots are associated with mantle upwelling; not all have an established deep plume origin.
The late Palaeozoic–Mesozoic supercontinent. Not the only one in Earth history.
The descent of one lithospheric plate beneath another into the mantle at a convergent boundary, commonly involving oceanic lithosphere.
A submarine mountain system at a spreading boundary, where mantle upwelling and melting form new oceanic crust. Seafloor generally becomes older away from the spreading axis.

misconception.claim: Continents plough through a static ocean floor.
misconception.truth: Continents are passengers on plates. Ocean floor is also plate, created at ridges and destroyed at trenches.

misconceptions.claim: Continents plough through a static ocean floor.
misconceptions.truth: Continents are passengers on plates. Ocean floor is also plate, created at ridges and destroyed at trenches.

misconceptions.claim: The UK is its own plate.
misconceptions.truth: The UK sits on the Eurasian plate. Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a divergent boundary.

misconceptions.claim: All volcanoes sit on plate edges.
misconceptions.truth: Most do. Hawaii is a hotspot punching through a plate interior. The age chain records plate motion.

teacher.script:
Begin with the model paused. Rotate the present-day globe. Teal marks divergent boundaries, coral convergent boundaries, and sand transform boundaries. Switch to Boundary section to compare their motion.

Ask students to predict the result before changing a control. Scrub the globe back towards Pangaea using 10 Ma GPlates snapshots. These are modern coastlines carried by a plate-motion model, not ancient shorelines. Return to 0 Ma to locate Hawaii.

Invite a student or geography club member to explain the comparison using the terms in this lab. Past views move modern coastlines using a plate model, so they show continental positions rather than ancient shorelines. Finish with a question from Check and ask for the evidence behind each answer.
pitfalls: Calling the UK a plate. It sits on the Eurasian plate.
Drawing arrows that point at the boundary instead of along plate motion.

modelNotes: The globe uses Bird PB2002 present-day boundaries; the past uses GPlates MULLER2019 coastlines reconstructed in a mantle reference frame.
Use the time slider for discrete 10 Ma snapshots.
If 3D is unavailable, use the photographs and the World map studio.

labs.title: Contours ↔ 3D terrain
labs.hook: A contour joins places at the same elevation.
labs.objective: Read contour lines as a 3D surface, tell spur from valley, and drop a spot height that matches the 3D hill.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Toggle 2D map and 3D hill. Same land. The V of the contours points up-valley; the spur’s V points downslope.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change the contour interval. Drop a spot height. Tight lines are steep. Wide lines are gentle.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain what changed and why. The same constructed terrain appears in both views, so changing the contour interval changes the map’s detail, not the hill.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Contour lines that form a V pointing uphill usually mark a…
questions.explain: Water flows out of the V. Valley contours point upstream (uphill).

choices: A ridge of high ground poking into lower ground; contour Vs point downhill.
questions.explain: Spur and valley are opposites in how the Vs point.

questions.prompt: If the contour interval is 10 m and you cross five contour intervals between two spots, the height difference is…
questions.explain: Five intervals × 10 m = 50 m. Count the gaps, not just the lines.
Steep = packed lines. Gentle = open lines. A cliff may show as coincident lines or a symbol.

why: A contour joins places at the same elevation. Closely spaced contours indicate a steep slope, while wider spacing indicates a gentler slope; their patterns reveal valleys, ridges and summits.
Change the contour interval. Drop a spot height. Tight lines are steep. Wide lines are gentle.
The same constructed terrain appears in both views, so changing the contour interval changes the map’s detail, not the hill.

glossary.def: Line joining points of equal height above datum.
The height step between adjacent contours.
A surveyed point with a printed elevation.
A ridge of high ground. Contours V downhill.
Low ground, often with a stream. Contours V uphill.
A small isolated hill: closed contour loops.

misconception.claim: Contours are paths.
misconception.truth: They are height. A path may follow a contour, but the line itself is not a trail.

misconceptions.claim: Contours are paths.
misconceptions.truth: They are height. A path may follow a contour, but the line itself is not a trail.

misconceptions.claim: The V of a contour always points downhill.
misconceptions.truth: Valley Vs point uphill (upstream). Spur Vs point downhill. Same ink, opposite jobs.

misconceptions.claim: You count the brown lines to get the height change.
misconceptions.truth: Count the intervals (gaps) and multiply by the contour interval. Five gaps at 10 m is 50 m.

teacher.script:
Begin with the model paused. Toggle 2D map and 3D hill. Same land. The V of the contours points up-valley; the spur’s V points downslope.

Ask students to predict the result before changing a control. Change the contour interval. Drop a spot height. Tight lines are steep. Wide lines are gentle.

Invite a student or geography club member to explain the comparison using the terms in this lab. The same constructed terrain appears in both views, so changing the contour interval changes the map’s detail, not the hill. Finish with a question from Check and ask for the evidence behind each answer.
pitfalls: Students counting lines instead of intervals.
Assuming north is always ‘up the slope’.

modelNotes: OS 1:25 000 and USGS quads both hide the hill in the interval.
What moves in this lab: the interval slider, the 2D/3D flip.
Vertical scale is readable, not a 1:1 mountain.
Flip 2D to 3D and the same V must still be a valley.
Change interval from 5 m to 20 m and ask what disappeared.
Vertical scale is readable, not a 1:1 mountain.
Without the 3D view: packed lines are steep, open lines are gentle, a V pointing upslope is a valley, a spur bends the other way.
That is enough for Check, and enough to sit an OS extract without the 3D crutch.

labs.title: River long profile
labs.hook: A river’s long profile usually becomes gentler downstream.
labs.objective: Follow a river from source to mouth, compare downstream gradients and bends, and distinguish discharge from stage.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Follow the bed from the steeper upper reach through bends to the gentler lower reach. These are parts of one river.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Raise Discharge and compare stage and wetted margins. Play follows water downstream without eroding the fixed channel.

steps.title: Explain
