steps.body: Explain what changed and why. The channel shape stays fixed while the water level changes; the displayed wet margins are an illustration rather than a mapped flood extent.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Where is vertical erosion most important?
questions.explain: Steep gradient, high potential energy, V-shaped valleys and waterfalls.

choices: A meander neck is cut off, usually in flood, and the old loop is abandoned.
questions.explain: Helicoidal flow erodes the outer bank. The neck thins. A cutoff shortens the river.

choices: Raises competence and can put water onto the floodplain.
Turns the river into a glacier.
questions.explain: Competence is the largest grain the flow can move. More discharge, more ability — up to a point.

choices: A river dropping load as it enters stiller water, faster than tides/waves can remove it.
questions.explain: Mississippi: huge load, modest tides. Many UK upland rivers never build a classic delta.

why: A river’s long profile usually becomes gentler downstream. Channel shape, water supply and sediment change along its course, helping explain why steep valleys and broad floodplains occur in different reaches.
Raise Discharge and compare stage and wetted margins. Play follows water downstream without eroding the fixed channel.
The channel shape stays fixed while the water level changes; the displayed wet margins are an illustration rather than a mapped flood extent.

glossary.def: The variation in river-bed elevation along a river from its source towards its mouth.
Largest particle the flow can move.
A bend in a river channel. Outer-bank erosion and inner-bank deposition commonly move the bend across a floodplain; a cutoff can leave an oxbow lake.
A curved former meander channel separated from the main river. It may contain an oxbow lake or gradually fill with sediment.
A raised bank beside a river, either built naturally by overbank sediment deposition or constructed to reduce flooding. Also written levee.
A body of sediment built where a river enters a sea or lake and deposits enough material to accumulate. Distributary channels often cross its surface.

misconception.claim: Rivers always take the shortest path to the sea.
misconception.truth: They meander on low gradients. The shortest path is a cutoff after a flood, not the default.

misconceptions.claim: Rivers always take the shortest path to the sea.
misconceptions.truth: They meander on low gradients. The shortest path is a cutoff after a flood, not the default.

misconceptions.claim: Upper, middle and lower course are three different rivers.
misconceptions.truth: They are stations on one long profile. Energy and load change downstream.

misconceptions.claim: Every UK river ends in a delta like the Mississippi.
misconceptions.truth: Many UK mouths are estuaries because of tides. A classic delta needs a large load and modest tidal range.

teacher.script:
Begin with the model paused. Follow the bed from the steeper upper reach through bends to the gentler lower reach. These are parts of one river.

Ask students to predict the result before changing a control. Raise Discharge and compare stage and wetted margins. Play follows water downstream without eroding the fixed channel.

Invite a student or geography club member to explain the comparison using the terms in this lab. The channel shape stays fixed while the water level changes; the displayed wet margins are an illustration rather than a mapped flood extent. Finish with a question from Check and ask for the evidence behind each answer.
pitfalls: Teaching the upper/middle/lower courses as three different rivers.
Forgetting that UK ‘deltas’ are often estuaries because of tides.

labs.title: Water cycle stores and flows
labs.hook: Water moves between the atmosphere, land and ocean through evaporation, precipitation and flows at and below the surface.
labs.objective: Name the main stores and transfers, read a drainage-basin overlay, and see how human abstraction lowers a reservoir.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Stores: ocean, atmosphere, ice, groundwater, soil, lakes. Flows: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, interception, infiltration, runoff, groundwater flow.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Toggle the drainage-basin overlay. Open the abstraction tap and watch the reservoir fall. The ocean does not notice; the town does.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain what changed and why. The tracers identify transfer routes; their size and spacing do not measure the volume of water moving along each route.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The largest store of fresh water is…
questions.explain: Most water is ocean (salt). Of the fresh remainder, ice dominates; then groundwater; rivers are a trickle.

choices: Water soaking into the soil surface.
questions.explain: If the soil cannot take more, water runs off. That is the flood story.

questions.prompt: Abstraction in this lab lowers the reservoir because…
choices: A local store is being mined faster than precipitation and inflow refill it.
questions.explain: Closed globally, open locally. Groundwater and reservoirs can be over-drawn.

choices: The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by a watershed.
questions.explain: The watershed is the divide. Rain on one side goes to this river; on the other side, another.

why: Water moves between the atmosphere, land and ocean through evaporation, precipitation and flows at and below the surface. Naming the stores first makes it easier to trace where water comes from and where it goes.
Toggle the drainage-basin overlay. Open the abstraction tap and watch the reservoir fall. The ocean does not notice; the town does.
The tracers identify transfer routes; their size and spacing do not measure the volume of water moving along each route.

glossary.def: A place water sits: ocean, ice, aquifer, lake, soil, air.
A flow between stores.
In UK geography, the drainage divide separating basins. In US usage, watershed commonly means the entire drainage basin; check the context.
Human removal of water from a store.
Rain caught on vegetation before it hits the ground.
The typical time material remains in a store. For a well-mixed store at steady state, mean residence time is its amount divided by its outflow rate.
Evaporation plus transpiration. A land transfer back to air.

misconception.claim: Water is used up.
misconception.truth: The global mass is conserved. Quality, location, and timing change. A dry reservoir is a local budget failure.

misconceptions.claim: Water is used up.
misconceptions.truth: The global mass is conserved. Quality, location, and timing change. A dry reservoir is a local budget failure.

misconceptions.claim: Rivers are a major global store of fresh water.
misconceptions.truth: Ice then groundwater dominate fresh water. Rivers are a fast transfer, a trickle in the budget.

misconceptions.claim: The cycle is a circle of arrows with no stores.
misconceptions.truth: Stores first, then transfers. Abstraction mines a named store. A flood is a transfer the soil cannot take.

teacher.script:
Begin with the model paused. Stores: ocean, atmosphere, ice, groundwater, soil, lakes. Flows: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, interception, infiltration, runoff, groundwater flow.

Ask students to predict the result before changing a control. Toggle the drainage-basin overlay. Open the abstraction tap and watch the reservoir fall. The ocean does not notice; the town does.

labs.title: Atmosphere as a thin film
labs.hook: Atmospheric layers are distinguished mainly by how temperature changes with altitude.
labs.objective: Name the main layers, state that weather is tropospheric, and read a lapse rate as temperature falling with height.

questions.prompt: Where does almost all weather happen?

choices: Temperature falls about 6.5 °C each kilometre up in the troposphere, on average.
questions.explain: Environmental lapse rate is a fall of temperature with height, on average, in the troposphere.

choices: Closer to the Sun in kilometres that matter.
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet and heats that layer.
It is closer to space heaters.
questions.explain: Ozone absorption, not ‘closer to the Sun’ in any useful sense.

choices: No — it is already in space.
Yes. The tropopause is still many kilometres above the city.
No, because air is 100% oxygen there.

why: Atmospheric layers are distinguished mainly by how temperature changes with altitude. Most weather occurs in the troposphere, while absorption of ultraviolet radiation helps warm the stratosphere above it.
Open Temperature profile. At lapse rate 6.5 °C/km, calculate 15 − 12 × 6.5 = −63 °C. Change the lapse rate to 4 °C/km and compare −33 °C.

glossary.def: The lowest atmospheric layer, containing most air mass and nearly all weather. It is typically about 8 km deep near the poles and 16–18 km near the tropics.
The boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere, identified mainly by a change in the vertical temperature gradient. Its altitude varies with latitude and weather.
How temperature changes with height. A positive environmental lapse usually means it gets colder up.
Layer above the tropopause, heated by ozone absorbing ultraviolet.
The atmospheric layer roughly 50–85 km above the surface, in which temperature generally falls with altitude. Many meteors become luminous here.
The very thin atmospheric layer above roughly 85 km where kinetic temperature generally rises with altitude as gases absorb energetic solar radiation. Much auroral activity occurs here.
Balloon-borne package that profiles temperature, humidity and pressure with height.
Region of higher ozone in the stratosphere that absorbs ultraviolet and heats that layer.

misconception.claim: Space begins just above the clouds.
misconception.truth: Clouds are in a thin film. There is a lot of atmosphere above them, but almost no weather.

misconceptions.claim: Space begins just above the clouds.
misconceptions.truth: Clouds are in a thin film. There is a lot of atmosphere above them, but almost no weather.

misconceptions.claim: The troposphere is about half the stack.
misconceptions.truth: On a fair drawing it is a film. School shells are exploded so you can name them, not so you can measure thickness from the poster.

misconceptions.claim: We run out of air at the tropopause, so Denver is halfway to space.
misconceptions.truth: Pressure falls with height, but air continues. Denver at about 1.6 km is still deep in a 10–12 km troposphere.

Pressure-gradient force: the force per unit mass associated with a pressure difference, directed from higher towards lower pressure.
PGF balanced by Coriolis. Friction neglected. Flow along the isobars.
Surface drag that slows the wind, weakens Coriolis, and lets PGF pull across isobars toward low.
